notes: PZPR holds ruling slot 4. Moczar's Partisans sit in 7 as the security-apparatus power bloc (largest popularity after PZPR); Gierek's Silesian Group in 13; Mijał's Maoist KPP in 19; the Commandos in 5; PAX (Piasecki) in 6. Western slots hold real opposition/exile bodies: Zaleski's government-in-exile (April Constitution legitimism) in 0, Znak in 1, Kultura in 2, exile PPS in 3 (MD's modern PPS slot 5 not followed, since the exile PPS was moderate social democratic). Satellite parties: SD in 16 (craftsmen and private sector), ZSL in 18 (peasant party). Church hierarchy in 14. Slots 8, 9, 11, 12 are Arab/Iraqi student circles; 10 is the real Tatar Muslim Religious Union.

0.name: Rząd Rzeczypospolitej Polskiej na uchodźstwie
0.text:
The Polish Government-in-Exile in London still claims to be the only lawful authority of the Polish state, deriving its legitimacy from the authoritarian April Constitution of 1935. President August Zaleski, in office since 1947 and backed by the old Piłsudskiite Sanacja camp, refused to step down in 1954 and is opposed by the rival Council of Three of General Władysław Anders and Edward Raczyński, which most émigré parties support.

The 'Castle' government stands for an independent, anti-communist Poland within the Western alliance, the eastern borders of 1939 and a strong presidency above parties. It has lost almost all foreign recognition, but it commands the loyalty of many veterans, keeps the pre-war state symbols and archives, and offers a ready-made legal framework should communist rule collapse.

1.name: Znak
1.text:
Znak is the small group of independent Catholic deputies admitted to the Sejm after the thaw of 1956, together with the Clubs of Catholic Intelligentsia, the Kraków weekly Tygodnik Powszechny and the Warsaw monthly Więź. Led by the lawyer Stanisław Stomma, with Tadeusz Mazowiecki among its deputies, it alone protested in parliament against the repression of students in March 1968 and has since been treated with open hostility.

Znak practises a cautious 'neo-positivism': loyal acceptance of Poland's geopolitical situation combined with steady pressure for civil liberties, religious freedom, the rule of law and openness to Western Europe and the Second Vatican Council. Its base is the Catholic intelligentsia of Kraków and Warsaw, and its leverage lies in its moral authority and its links to Cardinal Wyszyński and Western Christian Democrats.

2.name: Kultura
2.text:
Kultura is the monthly of the Literary Institute, edited since 1947 by Jerzy Giedroyc from a house in Maisons-Laffitte near Paris. Smuggled into Poland and passed from hand to hand among the intelligentsia, it is the freest Polish voice in the world, publishing banned writers from Czesław Miłosz to Witold Gombrowicz, while Juliusz Mieroszewski writes its political essays.

Kultura rejects both communism and the nostalgic émigré right. It argues for a democratic, pluralist and Western-oriented Poland that accepts its new eastern borders, reconciles with Germans, Ukrainians, Lithuanians and Belarusians, and wins freedom through gradual evolution rather than war. Its leverage lies in ideas: it shapes the thinking of dissidents, Catholic intellectuals and even reform-minded party members, and builds bridges to Western opinion.

3.name: Polska Partia Socjalistyczna
3.text:
The Polish Socialist Party, founded in 1892, was absorbed into the communist party in 1948, when Józef Cyrankiewicz, now prime minister, delivered its domestic organisation to the merger. Its independent wing survives in exile in London, led by Adam Ciołkosz, a pre-war deputy respected in the Socialist International, while former socialists inside the ruling party quietly remember their own heritage.

The exile PPS stands for a sovereign, democratic Poland with parliamentary government, free trade unions, workers' self-management and social ownership of key industries, anchored in Western Europe. It opposes Soviet domination and the émigré right alike. Its leverage lies in its ties to Western labour movements and in the memory of the party of Piłsudski and Daszyński among older workers.

4.name: Polska Zjednoczona Partia Robotnicza
4.text:
The Polish United Workers' Party has ruled Poland since its creation in 1948. Its First Secretary Władysław Gomułka, returned to power on a wave of popular hope in October 1956, has become an austere and suspicious ruler relying on a narrow circle around Zenon Kliszko, with Józef Cyrankiewicz as prime minister. The purges of 1968 and the invasion of Czechoslovakia have hardened the regime, while meat shortages and stagnant wages breed discontent.

The party upholds the leading role of the communists, the alliance with the Soviet Union and the Warsaw Pact, tolerating private farming and a strong Church as concessions of the Polish road. Gomułka's priority is a treaty with West Germany recognising the Oder–Neisse border. Its leverage is total: the state, the economy, the media and the security forces.

5.name: Komandosi
5.text:
The Commandos are the young rebels of Warsaw University, named for their habit of descending on official meetings with awkward questions. Inspired by Jacek Kuroń and Karol Modzelewski, whose Open Letter to the Party of 1965 denounced the bureaucracy in Marxist terms, and led by students such as Adam Michnik, they sparked the protests of March 1968. Today their leaders are in prison or have been driven into emigration by the anti-Zionist purge.

The Commandos demand freedom of speech, workers' councils, an end to censorship and a socialism without party bureaucrats. They reject both Soviet tutelage and the nationalism of the Partisans. Their leverage lies in their network among students and intellectuals, their contacts with the Western New Left and the moral force of their trials.

6.name: Stowarzyszenie PAX
6.text:
The PAX Association is a licensed movement of 'progressive Catholics' founded after the war by Bolesław Piasecki, the pre-war leader of the fascist ONR-Falanga, who made his peace with the Soviet security organs in 1945. It owns a publishing empire, profitable enterprises and seats in the Sejm, and in 1968 it joined Mieczysław Moczar's Partisans in the anti-Zionist campaign against revisionists and Jews.

PAX preaches a fusion of Catholic faith, Polish nationalism and socialism, combined with absolute loyalty to the Soviet alliance as the guarantor of Poland's western border. It is hostile to Cardinal Wyszyński's independence, to the Znak liberals and to Western influence. Its leverage lies in money, newspapers, regime patronage and Piasecki's ambition to become the Catholic partner of a nationalist communist leadership.

7.name: Partyzanci
7.text:
The Partisans are the faction of Mieczysław Moczar, a wartime communist guerrilla commander, Minister of the Interior from 1964 to 1968 and now a Central Committee secretary. Built on veterans of the communist underground organised in his ZBoWiD veterans' union and on officers of the Security Service, they drove the anti-Zionist campaign of 1968 that purged the party, universities and army of Jews and revisionists.

The Partisans offer a nationalist, authoritarian communism: Polish patriotism, the cult of the wartime partisan, hostility to Jews, intellectuals and 'cosmopolitans', and the firm hand of the security apparatus, all within the Soviet alliance. They are waiting for Gomułka to falter. Their leverage lies in police files, the veterans' movement, friendly editors and the resentment of younger cadres blocked by the old guard.

8.name: Krąg Falsafatuna
8.text:
The Falsafatuna Circle is a small group of Iraqi Shia students at Polish universities and polytechnics, sent on scholarships to study engineering, medicine and economics. In the dormitories of Warsaw, Kraków and Gdańsk they meet to read Our Philosophy and Our Economics, the books in which Muhammad Baqir al-Sadr of Najaf answers Marxism with an Islamic theory of society.

The circle seeks a modern, rational Shiism able to compete with communism and secular nationalism on their own ground, stressing social justice, education and the dignity of believers. It is wary of both the atheist state around it and the Ba'athist regime at home. It has no organisation beyond private meetings; its leverage lies in the future careers of its members and their links to the seminaries of Najaf.

9.name: Synowie Nadżafu
9.text:
The Sons of Najaf are a few militant Iraqi Shia students in Poland linked to the clandestine Islamic Dawa Party, founded in Najaf in the late 1950s to fight secularism and communism. The Ba'athist assault on the Najaf seminaries in 1969, when the regime expelled Iranian clerics and accused a son of Grand Ayatollah Muhsin al-Hakim of espionage, has turned their piety into anger.

The group believes that Islamic jurists must guide the state and that Muslims must organise in secret cells to overthrow godless regimes. It hates the Ba'ath, communism, Israel and the Shah's alliance with America alike. In Poland it hides carefully from the security police; its leverage lies in its discipline and in couriers to the underground Dawa network in Iraq.

10.name: Muzułmański Związek Religijny
10.text:
The Muslim Religious Union is the official body of the Polish Tatars, descendants of warriors who settled in the Grand Duchy of Lithuania from the fourteenth century and served the Commonwealth for centuries. Founded in Vilnius in 1925 and revived after the war, it now serves a few thousand faithful, centred on the wooden mosques of Bohoniki and Kruszyniany near Białystok and on resettled communities in Gdańsk and Warsaw.

The Union practises a quiet, establishment Sunni Islam and loyalty to the Polish state, mindful of the Tatars' long service in the Polish cavalry. Under communist rule it confines itself to religious life, cemeteries and the preservation of its heritage, while keeping discreet contacts with Muslim countries. Its leverage is small but symbolic, resting on its unique place in Poland's history.

11.name: Krąg Wyzwolenia
11.text:
The Liberation Circle is a secretive cell of Jordanian and Palestinian students at Polish medical and technical schools who follow Hizb ut-Tahrir, the Party of Liberation founded in Jerusalem in 1953 by Sheikh Taqiuddin al-Nabhani. Its pamphlets arrive through party members studying in West Germany and Austria and are copied by hand in student hostels.

The circle teaches that the Muslim world must be united under a restored caliphate, that every existing Arab regime is illegitimate and that capitalism and communism are equally systems of unbelief. It despises the Soviet-backed Arab nationalists as much as the West and Israel. Under the eyes of the Polish security service it stays tiny and silent; its leverage lies only in the conviction of its members.

12.name: Muzułmański Krąg Studencki
12.text:
The Muslim Student Circle gathers devout Syrian, Egyptian and Sudanese students in Poland, many from families persecuted by the Ba'athist and Nasserist regimes, for Friday prayers, Quran study and mutual aid. It follows the ideas of the Muslim Brotherhood and draws its literature from Said Ramadan's Islamic Centre in Geneva and Brotherhood exiles in West Germany.

The circle reads Hassan al-Banna and Sayyid Qutb, hanged in Cairo in 1966, and hopes for an Islamic order built through preaching, education and lawful organisation. It rejects atheist communism, secular Arab nationalism and Western materialism alike, while keeping on good terms with the Polish Tatars, whose mosques it sometimes visits. Its leverage is modest: the loyalty of a few dozen future doctors and engineers who will return home.

13.name: Grupa śląska
13.text:
The Silesian Group is the following of Edward Gierek, party First Secretary of Katowice province since 1957 and a member of the Politburo. A former miner who spent his youth in France and Belgium, Gierek has turned Upper Silesia into a showcase of efficient management, new housing and better-supplied shops, and his loyal Katowice apparatus is increasingly seen as a government in waiting.

The group favours pragmatic, consumer-oriented modernisation over Gomułka's austerity: industrial investment financed by Western credits and licences, better wages, technical expertise and a more polished style of rule. It is loyal to Moscow and wary of the Partisans' adventurism, though willing to work with them against the old guard. Its leverage lies in Silesian coal and steel, efficient cadres and the respect of the Soviet leadership.

14.name: Episkopat Polski
14.text:
The Catholic Church, to which the vast majority of Poles belong, is the only mass institution in the country beyond the party's control. Its Primate, Cardinal Stefan Wyszyński, imprisoned from 1953 to 1956, led the Great Novena and the Millennium celebrations of 1966 that drew millions in open rivalry with the state, while Cardinal Karol Wojtyła of Kraków is a rising voice of the episcopate.

The bishops defend religious education, church building, Catholic publishing and the rights of the faithful, and present themselves as guardians of the nation's soul rather than a political opposition. They distrust both communist atheism and Western consumerism. Their leverage is immense: the pulpits, the loyalty of the countryside and the Church's role as the voice of a nation without free institutions.

15.name: Czerwoni dyrektorzy
15.text:
The Red Directors are the managers of Poland's great state combines and industrial associations: the Lenin Steelworks at Nowa Huta, the coal mines of Upper Silesia, the shipyards of Gdańsk, Gdynia and Szczecin, the chemical works and the foreign trade enterprises. Party members to a man, they owe their posts to the nomenklatura, yet run their empires as personal fiefdoms with privileged access to cars, flats and foreign travel.

They want investment, imported Western machinery and freedom from the planners in Warsaw, and they resist both workers' self-management and the cost-cutting of Gomułka's new incentive system. Their leverage lies in their control of production, exports and hundreds of thousands of jobs, and in the ministries and provincial party bosses who depend on their results.

16.name: Stronnictwo Demokratyczne
16.text:
The Democratic Party was founded in 1939 by liberal intellectuals and survives as one of the two licensed allies of the communists in the Front of National Unity. It holds seats in the Sejm and the Council of State and represents craftsmen, shopkeepers, private traders, doctors, lawyers and the technical intelligentsia, the remnants of the private urban middle class.

Publicly it endorses socialism and the leading role of the party; privately its members defend private enterprise in crafts and services, lower taxes on small businesses, professional autonomy and the rule of law. It looks back with pride to the democratic traditions of the interwar intelligentsia. Its leverage is limited but real: it is the only legal channel for the interests of the private sector and the free professions.

17.name: Liga Ochrony Przyrody
17.text:
The League for Nature Protection was founded in 1928 and has become a mass organisation with hundreds of thousands of members, many of them schoolchildren organised in school circles. Working alongside the State Council for Nature Protection and scientists of the Polish Academy of Sciences, it promotes national parks, reserves and the protection of species such as the European bison of Białowieża.

A new generation of members is alarmed by the price of forced industrialisation: the poisoned air of Upper Silesia and Kraków, the dying Vistula and forests killed by industrial fumes. The League urges stricter pollution controls and planning that respects nature, without challenging the system directly. Its leverage lies in its size, its scientific allies and the sympathy of a public that sees its landscapes despoiled.

18.name: Zjednoczone Stronnictwo Ludowe
18.text:
The United People's Party was created in 1949 by merging the remnants of Stanisław Mikołajczyk's Polish People's Party with the communist-controlled peasant party, and serves as the junior partner of the communists in the Front of National Unity. Led by Czesław Wycech, a veteran of the pre-war peasant movement and Marshal of the Sejm, it holds over a hundred parliamentary seats and ministries dealing with agriculture.

The party represents Poland's millions of private smallholders, who kept their land when collectivisation was abandoned in 1956. It presses for better procurement prices, fertiliser, machinery, rural credit and pensions for farmers, while invoking the traditions of Wincenty Witos and the peasant movement. Its leverage lies in the countryside's weight in food supply and the regime's need to keep the peasants quiet.

19.name: Komunistyczna Partia Polski
19.text:
The Communist Party of Poland is an illegal Maoist party founded in 1965 by Kazimierz Mijał, a former minister and Stalinist hardliner who broke with Gomułka over 'revisionism' and sided with Beijing in the Sino-Soviet split. Mijał fled to Albania in 1966 and directs the party from Tirana, whose radio broadcasts its programme while couriers smuggle leaflets into Poland.

The party denounces Gomułka and the Soviet leadership as revisionist traitors, glorifies Stalin, Mao Zedong and Enver Hoxha, and calls for a return to the dictatorship of the proletariat, collectivisation and class struggle. It has only small clandestine cells among old Stalinist cadres and disaffected workers, but its links to Beijing and Tirana and the appeal of radical purity give it a voice beyond its numbers.

20.name: Stronnictwo Narodowe
20.text:
The National Party is the political heir of Roman Dmowski's National Democracy, the largest force of the pre-war Polish right. Banned at home since the communist takeover, it survives in exile in London under its long-time chairman Tadeusz Bielecki, with branches among Polish émigrés in Britain, France and the Americas, while its old supporters in Poland remain scattered and silent.

The party stands for a Catholic Polish nation, private property, the family and a strong state, combined with deep hostility to both Germany and Soviet Russia. It opposes the Sanacja-backed exile president and distrusts liberal émigrés. Its leverage lies in the persistence of national-democratic ideas among older Poles and in the way the regime's own Partisans have borrowed its nationalist language.

21.name: Mieczyk Chrobrego
21.text:
Chrobry's Sword takes its name from the sword badge worn by the radical nationalist youth of the 1930s, from the Camp of Great Poland to the National Radical Camp, banned by the government in 1934. Its heirs are scattered veterans of the ONR and the wartime National Armed Forces, mostly in exile, and a handful of young sympathisers at home who read pre-war tracts in secret.

They dream of a Catholic, ethnically pure Greater Poland ruled by a disciplined national elite, free of communists, Jews, Germans and Russians alike. They despise the exile democrats and regard Piasecki's collaboration with the regime as betrayal. Their numbers are negligible and the security police hunts any sign of them, but the anti-Semitic campaign of 1968 showed that their ideas still echo.

22.name: Ludowe Wojsko Polskie
22.text:
The Polish People's Army, the second largest force of the Warsaw Pact, has been led since April 1968 by the Minister of National Defence, General Wojciech Jaruzelski, a disciplined officer who joined the communist-led Polish forces in the Soviet Union in 1943. Its units took part in the invasion of Czechoslovakia in August 1968, and the anti-Zionist purge removed many Jewish officers from its ranks.

The army sees itself as the guardian of Poland's western border, the socialist order and the alliance with the Soviet Union, but also cultivates Polish military traditions and a professional esprit de corps. Political officers keep watch on the ranks. Its leverage lies in its size, its discipline and the confidence of Moscow, which could make it the arbiter in a crisis of the party.

23.name: Habsburgowie żywieccy
23.text:
The Żywiec Habsburgs are the Polonised branch of the House of Habsburg-Lorraine. Archduke Charles Stephen, master of the Żywiec estates, was considered for the throne of the Kingdom of Poland proclaimed by the Central Powers in 1916, and his son Archduke Charles Albert served as a Polish officer and refused German nationality in 1939. Dispossessed by the communists, the family now lives in Sweden and Switzerland.

Polish monarchism is a faint idea kept alive by small émigré circles who see a Catholic constitutional crown as a symbol above party strife and a bridge to Central Europe. A restored kingdom would stand for Catholic tradition, national unity and Western orientation. Its leverage is purely sentimental, resting on the family's patriotic record and memories of the Regency Kingdom.
